item.question: What do these names mean? Once you count their faces, you will know.
steps_tex: Count the faces of the icosahedron one by one, ticking each face once: there are $20$.
Count the faces of the dodecahedron the same way: there are $12$.

Check: the names give $20$ and $12$, and your ticks gave the same counts.

item.question: How many edges do you see? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___ How did you count them such that you do not miss out any edge or count an edge twice?
steps_tex: Count the sides of all the faces. Icosahedron: $20$ faces with $3$ sides each, so $20 \times 3 = 60$ sides.
Dodecahedron: $12$ faces with $5$ sides each, so $12 \times 5 = 60$ sides.
An edge is a side of $2$ faces, so every edge was counted twice. Halve each count.
Icosahedron: $60 \div 2 = 30$ edges. Dodecahedron: $60 \div 2 = 30$ edges.
Check: every edge is shared by exactly $2$ faces, so no edge is missed and none is counted twice.

item.question: Can you think of any other solid shapes that have faces that look the same? Do the same number of faces meet at each common vertex?
steps_tex: Think of a solid whose faces are all the same. A cube is one: a dice has the shape of a cube.
A cube has $6$ faces and all of them are squares of the same size.
Count the faces at one corner of the cube: $3$ faces meet there.
Try another corner: again $3$ faces meet. So yes, the same number of faces meet at every vertex of a cube.
Check: the cube has $8$ corners and $3$ faces meet at each one.

item.question: You can also build some solid shapes using straws or ice-cream sticks and clay or play dough. Which shapes did you make?
steps_tex: Choose a solid to build, for example a cube. A cube has $12$ edges and $8$ corners.
Each straw is one edge, so use $12$ straws. Each ball of clay is one corner, so use $8$ balls.
Put a ball of clay at the end of every straw and join $3$ straws at each ball.
Check: $8$ balls with $3$ straws each give $8 \times 3 = 24$ straw ends, and $12$ straws have $12 \times 2 = 24$ ends. The counts match.
